beats.narration_text: Every earnings call is dressed in careful non-answers — I'm Anjana, and I don't buy them. ECIS reads straight through the hedge language and tells you what a company actually meant, with a confidence score that gets graded against reality thirty days later. Here's how it works — and why it's willing to admit when it's wrong.

output lines resolve: 'reads every hedge phrase, four ways' / 'confidence: 0.87 — and it's checked later' / 'wrong calls get logged too'

props.command: Every earnings call is full of sentences built to say as little as possible — "we remain cautiously optimistic about our forward outlook." Can you build me something that reads the transcript and tells me whether guidance was actually raised, lowered, or held — with a confidence score I can actually trust, and a record of whether it turned out to be right?
output: reads every hedge phrase, four ways

beats.narration_text: Here's the line: "we remain cautiously optimistic about our forward outlook." Did that company just raise guidance? Lower it? Or say absolutely nothing at all? A room full of analysts will argue about it for an hour. ECIS reads it and answers — automatically, with a confidence score you can actually trust.

three labels stagger in below the quote — 'Raised?' (amber) / 'Lowered?' (red) / 'Maintained?' (grey) — each pulses once
'Raised' locks in — grows, green highlight, confidence badge '0.87' animates in beside it

props.quote: We remain cautiously optimistic about our forward outlook.

beats.narration_text: Here is the problem. An earnings call transcript runs five to ten thousand words of hedged, legalistic language. A simple keyword search catches the obvious phrases but misses anything subtle. A single language model will hallucinate signals that are not there. And reading every transcript manually does not scale — not when you are tracking thirty to fifty companies every quarter.

show.event: dense transcript text wall scrolls vertically at high speed — too fast to read
on 'keyword search catches the obvious' — a phrase highlights green mid-scroll
on 'will hallucinate' — a different phrase gets a red strike-through, tagged 'hallucination'
on 'does not scale' — scroll accelerates hard, text blurs
freeze-frame on one ambiguous sentence, pulsing '?' overlay

beats.narration_text: ECIS doesn't trust one method — it runs four independent readers on every chunk. A keyword scanner catches known phrasing. FinBERT scores the tone. A named-entity model pulls the hard numbers — dollars, percentages, dates. And a language model reasons through the passage with its own checks built in. A triangulator fuses all four, weighting the readers that keep being right more than the ones that don't.

show.event: 'Transcript' document icon enters left, splits into chunk blocks
Keyword node (blue rectangle) draws in on 'keyword scanner'
FinBERT node (teal) draws in on 'FinBERT'
NER node (orange) draws in on 'named-entity model'
LLM node (purple) draws in on 'language model'

production_viz.label: Four-reader triangulation

beats.narration_text: Not every chunk needs the full treatment. An orchestration agent sorts each one into four categories. Category A, both readers agree, goes straight to the LLM for confirmation. Category B, one reader flagged something and the other didn't, gets the full pipeline. Category C, the readers disagree, routes to conflict resolution. And Category D, neither reader saw anything, gets skipped entirely — which alone cuts LLM calls by sixty to eighty percent.

beats.narration_text: Every signal is pre-registered — logged before anyone knows if it was right. Thirty days later, ECIS checks the market. The Brier score measures overall accuracy. The skill score asks if a reader beats a plain keyword search. Expected calibration error checks whether an eighty-percent call is actually right eighty percent of the time. And Murphy decomposition splits genuine uncertainty from a model that's just miscalibrated.

on 'skill score' — second cluster plots, label appears
on 'calibration error' — bins glow green (on diagonal) or amber (off), label appears

beats.narration_text: ECIS keeps learning after deployment. Three feedback loops run continuously — a calibration watchdog that recalibrates confidence as it drifts, a routing graph that checks whether skipped chunks actually had signal in them, and a vindication tracker that reweights the four readers based on who keeps being right. Routine adjustments happen on their own. Anything structural — reverting a model, dropping a reader, a threshold shift over twenty-five percent — pauses the system for a human to approve.

dividing line appears below all three loops
human silhouette icon appears at gate checkpoint; 'Approve' / 'Reject' buttons; Approve pulses once; label 'Structural changes require human approval'

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Four independent readers voting on every chunk. One scorecard that checks itself against the market thirty days later. Three feedback loops that keep the system honest. And a human who signs off before anything structural changes. That's ECIS.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. "I make a judgment call at work that I never actually track — I just trust my gut and move on. I watched how ECIS pre-registers every prediction before the outcome is known, then checks itself against reality thirty days later. Can you help me: one, design a simple log where I write down my call and my confidence before I know if I'm right; two, pick two independent ways to sanity-check the same call; and three, define one honest test for whether my confidence numbers actually mean anything?" Paste that into Claude and see what it proposes for your own pre-registration log — same discipline as the four readers, aimed at your own gut calls.
